intro: How to read a Japanese auction sheet before you bid. Grades vary a little between auctions and inspectors, so always get the whole sheet translated. Even a grade 4.5 car can hide one serious fault.
overall: Under a year from first registration. As new.
Near perfect. Very rare on a car more than 10 years old.
Excellent for its age, with a few small, easily fixed marks. Rare over 15 years old.
Above average. Some light fade or dents; usually under about 100,000 km.
The most common grade, with a very wide spread: burns, bigger dents, peeling paint. Typically 100,000–200,000 km. Read the notes carefully and get an inspection.
Poor overall, or a serious issue (rust, mechanical), or a minor accident that didn't need frame repair.
Very poor, often with rust holes. Mostly parts cars.
Heavily modified: engine or gearbox swap, big turbo, auto-to-manual conversion, race prep. Not an indication of condition.
Minor accident damage, well repaired. Otherwise can be as good as a 4.5. Worth an inspection. These are all minor-repair grades at different auctions.

Accident repaired, which can mean anything from small to major. Not the same as a UK write-off. Repairs show as XX on the diagram, but some are only mentioned in the Japanese notes, so get those translated.

Not inspected. It could be too old to grade, the seller chose the cheapest listing, an unrepaired accident, a non-runner, flood damage or unconfirmed modifications. Photos taken outdoors make accident or non-runner more likely. Ask for an inspection.
interior: Very nice: maybe dirty or a worn wheel/knob, but nothing really wrong.
Average for 15+ years old. A mixed bag, so check the notes.
Poor: cracked dash, sagging headlining, ripped or stained seats, missing trim. The big auctions rarely use these.
Some auctions add a second letter for the body/exterior, e.g. overall 4, exterior B, interior B.
damage: Size or severity: 1 smallest. Most auctions use 1–3, some go to 4.
Scratch or chip (A1 polishes out, A2 medium, A3 large: 10–50 cm or across panels)
Dent (U1 thumb-size, U2 palm-size, U3 larger)
Repaired or repainted (W1 good, W2 slight ripple, W3 poor: drips, mismatch, wrinkles). Inspectors sometimes mark W when unsure, so it may be invisible.
Crack or tear (Y1 thumb-size, Y2 palm-size, often 5–10 cm on bumpers, Y3 larger)
Rust (S1 fist-size, S2 larger). S in the written notes can mean underbody rust. C on the wheel arches suggests a snowy-region car.
Paint damage: peeling, drips (P2 usually needs a repaint)
Stone chip (often on the windscreen). Usually tiny, not a reason to replace the glass.
Combined, e.g. AU3 = large scratch with large dent, AY2 = medium scratch and crack
abbrev: Next to the mileage: not confirmed (old car, odometer swap, 5-digit clock). Often genuine, but get it checked.

why: Didn't reach the reserve, so it's listed again elsewhere or later
Cleaned up or repaired, then relisted for a better grade
Moved to a different auction to find better prices
check: Mileage must rise from sheet to sheet. Any drop is a big red flag for clocking.
Treat a sudden grade jump (e.g. R → 4.5) with suspicion: find out what was repaired.
Damage or frame notes on an earlier sheet shouldn't just disappear.
Ask for every previous sheet. A seller who won't show them may be hiding something.

tips: Most good cars go through a handful of big physical auctions with inspection agents: Tokyo, Nagoya, Osaka, Kobe and Fukuoka.
USS controls more than half of Japanese auction sales. TAA and smaller auctions are often cheaper, and dealers move cars from them to USS for a quick profit.
Fukuoka can be cheaper. Allow about ¥30,000 to move a car to Osaka for shipping.
Avoid Hokkaido/Sapporo cars: months of snow and salted roads mean rust, plus about ¥60,000 extra transport.
Online-only auctions (AUCNET, NPS) can't be physically inspected.
Previous-sale data services (e.g. JCHC) show a car's earlier grades and prices. Cars first time at auction are usually cheaper.

tips_extra: Factory recalls can be done free at a Toyota dealer in Japan before export. Ask your agent, as it's much easier than chasing them in the UK.
Rust isn't always on the sheet: even grade 4.5 cars can be rusty underneath. Ask for underbody photos.
Agents physically inspect at the big auctions: they run the engine, check the gearbox and A/C, and photograph underneath. Worth paying for.
